transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-21 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~62m | Attendees: Evan B, Priya N, Jorge M (Redwood) ; Alex R, Maya S, Tom W, Sasha L (Corvus)

[00:00] Evan Brooks: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're going to run through the benchmark methodology deck. i'll kick off with goals then priya will go deep on runtime stuff.
[00:18] Alex Rivera: cool, yeah we want an apples to apples baseline so we can compare on-prem runs with your dedicated offering, cost and p95 are main things.
[00:30] Priya Nair: yep, apples to apples is two things: identical model checkpoint + tokenizer, and identical prompt truncation / left-padding rules. a lot of noise comes from different tokenization or different eos handling.
[00:46] Maya Singh: quick Q, when you say identical model artifact, do you mean the exact same compiled kernels? we can't run redwood runtime on our air-gapped yet.
[00:58] Jorge Martinez: good call --- for on-prem we recommend using the same model weights file (S3 or scp transfer) and the same quantized artifact if you're doing quant. kernel selection may differ across cuda drivers, so we log kernel versions and include them in the workbook.
[01:18] Tom Wu: notation: our infra is H100 on prem, single node with 80GB. cloud runs will use a100-80g—should we care?
[01:28] Priya Nair: model perf will change with hardware; include GPU type as a labeled dimension. for apples-to-apples, make sure the batch config, sequence length distribution, and micro-batching settings match. document everything in the workbook.
[01:42] Alex Rivera: on KV cache — how much does warm vs cold kv affect p95 for short prompts?
[01:54] Priya Nair: a lot. short prompts typically benef from prefix/KV cache warmup. our recommendation: run two passes — cold start (no cache) and warm start (prefix cache primed, e.g., run warmup queries until KV cache hit rate stabilizes). capture p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec.
[02:13] Evan Brooks: and capture token generation time vs request latency separately — sometimes the SDK adds overhead.
[02:23] [crosstalk]
[02:36] Maya Singh: for load gen — do you prefer concurrency-based (n concurrent users) or RPS? we have both.
[02:45] Priya Nair: both matter. we typically run a mix: steady-state RPS ramps and concurrency-based tail tests. in practice: 1) short ramp to target RPS over 5-10 mins, 2) hold for 10-15 mins to capture steady-state, 3) blast tests for tail using bursts. include think-time distributions from prod traces if you have them.
[03:05] Alex Rivera: we'll share traces. we have a bimodal request size distribution — chat messages and summary jobs — should we separate them?
[03:16] Priya Nair: yes separate workload classes and report combined weighted metrics. apples-to-apples requires the same ratio in each run.
[03:27] Evan Brooks: let's talk quant: 4-bit vs int8 — how do you want us to structure tests?
[03:35] Jorge Martinez: recommend three tiers: FP16 baseline, 4-bit quant (LLM.int4 or similar) and int8. for each tier run the same prompt sets, measure quality (ROUGE/BLEU/LLM-judged) plus latency and token throughput. keep the sampling seed consistent.
[03:54] Alex Rivera: quality eval — we can run our golden prompt set and human spot-check 100 samples. is that fine?
[04:02] Priya Nair: perfect — capture exact prompts, outputs, and random seeds. note: some decoders introduce nondeterminism across kernels, document RNG settings.
[04:16] Tom Wu: there was mention of kernel selection earlier; can differing cudnn or driver cause regression in perplexity?
[04:25] Priya Nair: yes—different GEMM kernel choices can change numerical precision, especially with quant. again, log driver and runtime versions; include a reproducibility checklist.
[04:38] Sasha Lee: procurement Q — are you collecting IP or model weights during testing? we need clarity for legal.
[04:46] Evan Brooks: no, redwood does not retain customer model weights for hosted tests unless agreed; for dedicated/private we can run entirely in your VPC/on-prem. we'll share an SOC2 summary and an evidence list.
[05:00] [00:05] Evan checks a deck link: "benchmark workbook (drive.link/XX)"
[05:15] Maya Singh: network: we have egress firewall and a proxy; how do we avoid proxy-induced tail latency?
[05:22] Jorge Martinez: run a local loopback test for baseline network latency; for VPC tests, use the exact network path you expect in production and treat proxy overhead as part of system latency. also capture per-hop RTTs.
[05:38] Alex Rivera: for batching — what's the sweet spot? we have latency SLO 200ms p95 for chat messages (<=128 tokens) but want high throughput for batch summarization.
[05:52] Priya Nair: batching is a tradeoff: larger batches increase throughput and GPU utilization but increase queuing latency. strategies: dynamic batching with latency caps, or fixed micro-batching tuned to p95. test multiples: batch sizes [1,4,8,16] with a per-request latency cutoff and measure effective throughput.
[06:12] Tom Wu: does Redwood runtime support continuous batching and adaptive timeouts?
[06:18] Priya Nair: yes, we have continuous batching in the runtime and can configure max batch latency. we'll share recommended configs.
[06:27] Evan Brooks: let's define the baseline test matrix real quick so we can capture it in the workbook.
[06:33] Priya Nair: baseline matrix: model artifact (fp16/4bit/int8), hardware (H100/A100), KV cache state (cold/warm), batch sizes [1,4,8,16], prompt sets (chat short, chat long, batch summarization), load profile (ramp, steady, burst).
[06:51] Alex Rivera: sounds good. also we want cost-per-1k tokens metric. any tips?
[06:59] Jorge Martinez: compute tokens/sec * runtime cost per-minute; for on-prem convert to equivalent vGPU cost or amortized GPU runcost. include detailed assumptions.
[07:10] Maya Singh: how long to warm KV cache? we saw variability between 200 and 2k requests in prior tests.
[07:18] Priya Nair: depends on prompt diversity. if you have common prefixes, a few hundred unique prefixes may settle cache hit rate. capture cache hit rate over time and plot p95 as a function of hit rate.
[07:30] [audible typing]
[07:45] Alex Rivera: minor transcription noise — we might see "kv cash" in the auto transcripts historically, just note.
[07:53] Evan Brooks: haha yes fireflies mishears things a lot.
[08:01] Priya Nair: for apples-to-apples measuring tokenization align char-level lengths too. e.g., if one run uses different bpe merges, effective token lengths differ and latency changes.
[08:16] Tom Wu: any specific logging we should enable?
[08:22] Jorge Martinez: log request id, model version, kernel versions, batch size, kv hit/miss, token counts, decode time, host-level metrics (CPU, mem, NIC). also capture GPU SM utilization and memory ops.
[08:40] Maya Singh: about on-prem vs cloud: should we expect deterministic differences caused by PCI-e gen or CPU diff?
[08:48] Priya Nair: yes chain-level differences (PCI-e, interconnect) matter. include a hardware spec table and run microbenchmarks (memory copy, memcpy, kernel warms) to characterize baseline overhead.
[09:03] Alex Rivera: what about dataset leakage / PII during testing? we need to avoid sending sensitive customer PII to hosted endpoints.
[09:12] Evan Brooks: for hosted runs use redaction or hashed samples; for private runs keep everything on-prem. we'll share guidance doc.
[09:24] Sasha Lee: good. legal wants an evidence pack: audit logs, who accessed test creds, and a copy of config files. can you provide?
[09:33] Evan Brooks: yes. we'll package an evidence bundle for the pilot that includes logs and config.
[09:38] [10:00] --- mid-call recap ---
[10:05] Priya Nair: recap: 1) we agreed baseline matrix; 2) run cold and warm kv tests; 3) test fp16/4bit/int8 with quality eval; 4) log kernel/driver versions; 5) share workbook and schedule run.
[10:22] Alex Rivera: ok let's dive a little deeper on the quant quality checks.
[10:29] Jorge Martinez: when testing quant, capture delta metrics: exact-match rates for structured outputs, and LLM-eval scores for instruction prompts. avoid only automated metrics; include small human sample.
[10:41] Maya Singh: how should we handle nondeterministic decodes affecting quality scores?
[10:47] Priya Nair: freeze seeds where possible; for beams or sampling run multiple seeds and report variance. also compare distributional metrics not single-run.
[11:00] Alex Rivera: we also want to measure latency variance per token — some kernels spike at certain sequence lengths.
[11:08] Priya Nair: measure per-token latency by sequence-length buckets: <=64, 65-128, 129-512, >512. that surfaces knee points where kernel selection flips.
[11:20] Tom Wu: do you recommend single-token streaming for chat?
[11:25] Jorge Martinez: streaming reduces tail for interactive use; measure both chunked streaming and full-response latencies. streaming may reveal per-token jitter.
[11:36] [12:00] interruption, line noise - "uh-huh"
[12:12] Evan Brooks: ops note: for the VPC on-prem run we'll need a short-lived user with scp/ssh and a shared s3 endpoint or rsync. Jorge will outline the access pattern.
[12:24] Jorge Martinez: yes we'll do timeboxed access and ephemeral keys. document the data deletion plan.
[12:35] Alex Rivera: security folks want to validate KMS usage when we test quant artifacts stored in S3.
[12:44] Evan Brooks: we can support KMS/HSM and will record the usage in the evidence bundle.
[12:52] Sasha Lee: is there a change to SLA if we run on dedicated?
[12:58] Evan Brooks: dedicated contract gives SLA; private on-prem will be by arrangement. we can share the SLA excerpts.
[13:08] Maya Singh: one more nuance — for batch summarization we sometimes concat multiple docs into a single prompt which changes token distribution. ensure your load generator supports variable sequence sampling.
[13:20] Priya Nair: yes include sequence sampling in the runner; we'll share a sampling script.
[13:30] Alex Rivera: about apples-to-apples: should we pin random seeds, tokenizers, and model hashes in the workbook header?
[13:38] Priya Nair: absolutely. include checksums (sha256) of model files.
[13:44] Evan Brooks: any final concerns from legal or procurement?
[13:50] Sasha Lee: we'll need a one-pager that states what is and isn't retained during tests.
[13:56] Evan Brooks: we'll provide that.
[14:04] Priya Nair: final quick note on measurement noise: run each test at least 3 times and report median plus min/max and stddev. avoid single-run conclusions.
[14:16] Alex Rivera: great. sounds like a plan. thanks.
[14:22] Evan Brooks: next steps recap — we'll share workbook, scripts, and set up a short test window. I'll follow up with the calendar invite.
[14:30] [END]
